name: metric beside the figure but outside the quoted words is read from the letter

row.source_text: lvp, about 32 m2 of flooring, austin tx

why: This used to refuse, on the rule that only what the model copied counts. The rule guards against a unit invented out of nothing; it was costing the opposite -- a unit the customer wrote, standing immediately after the figure, thrown away because the quote stopped a word early. What is adjacent to the citation is not uncited text. A unit from another sentence is still refused, and has its own fixture.

name: staple-down over a slab needs a plywood subfloor first
why: Staple-down needs something to staple into. Over a concrete slab that means laying a plywood subfloor first, a different job at a different price, and no email can say whether it is needed.

name: a diagonal layout wastes more material than a straight one
why: A diagonal layout cuts more material off at every wall, so the same area costs more than the straight version at the standard rate. The formula does not know that, so the price may not go out on its own.

name: a material the price book does not carry cannot be quoted
why: The catalogue in the database is what the firm can actually price, not what the gate can recognise. A word it knows but the price book has no band for is a job for a human to answer, and saying so is the difference between a considered refusal and a silent one.

name: a number with nothing beside it is a question, not a default
why: Grounding proves the words are in the email; it cannot prove a number means square feet. A number with no unit written beside it is the one case the system must ask about rather than assume, because assuming is what turns 32 into a tenfold underquote.

name: the unit the customer wrote is read, and the number converted
why: When the email writes the unit out, the unit is a fact like any other and carries its own evidence. 32 m2 is 344 sq ft; storing 32 would price a tenth of the job.

why: Carpet is sold by the square yard in the US and a square yard is nine square feet. Reading the unit rather than assuming it is the difference between 40 and 360.

name: a mangled quote of the unit does not stop the letter from settling it
why: The model answered m2 as bytes carrying a NUL, so its own quote proves nothing. That is a transport fault, not a doubt about what the customer wrote: the letter says m² next to the figure and is not mangled. Control characters are still stripped before anything crosses into the database.

name: a quote that spans a line break is still the customer’s own words
why: Email wraps. A fragment the model copied across a line break is the same words the customer wrote, so it must ground. Deleting the newline instead of replacing it glues the words together and the gate accuses an honest quote of being invented — the worst way to be wrong, because a fabrication flag blocks the whole email.

name: dimensions with no unit on either side are a question too
why: The rule that a bare number must not be assumed to be square feet does not stop being true when the number arrives as a multiplication. Twelve by ten is a hundred and twenty of something, and nothing in the email says of what.

name: when the model's unit disagrees with the words it quoted, the letter decides
why: The model answered sqft while quoting m². Refusing was safe but blind; reading the letter is safer still, because it is the letter that says metres and the letter that the number came from. This is precisely the tenfold error the unit field exists to prevent, and it is prevented by believing the customer rather than the model.

name: the unit is read as the customer spells it, not as the schema names it
why: The model answers in the words of the email, and a person writes sq ft, not sqft. Demanding the schema's own spelling threw away a perfectly grounded unit and asked the customer for something they had already given — which is the failure the order layer exists to stop.

name: a new enquiry from someone quoted once before is not an acceptance
why: prior_offers counts every offer this contact has ever had, across years and jobs. A customer quoted for a bathroom last spring who writes about a bedroom now is starting again, and 'go ahead' cannot refer to a price nobody has sent them for this work. Only an offer in this exchange can be accepted.

row.source_text: hi again - go ahead and send me something for the bedroom, about 180 sq ft

name: a job with everything and no quote is priced, whatever the letter says

row.source_text: can you send me the price?

why: A conversation gives its facts across several letters. This one carries none of them and asks for nothing in particular, but the job behind it has a material, a size and a town, and nobody has quoted it. Sitting on a ready job because the newest letter is short is how a customer is lost to whoever answers first.

name: the same letter, once a quote has gone out, is a conversation to continue

row.source_text: can you send me the price?

why: The mirror of the case above, and the reason it is written as a pair. Once a price has been sent, the same words mean something else entirely -- a question about a quote they already have -- and quoting them a second time is worse than not answering.

name: a ready job is not asked for what it already holds

row.source_text: still interested

why: One row said the_job_is_ready and, in the same breath, that material, area and location were all still needed -- because it asked what this letter lacked rather than what the job lacked. Nothing prices from that field; the second reader is its only consumer, and it believed it and stopped a job that wanted nothing.

name: the town the job holds is not asked for again

row.source_text: laminate, about 400 sq ft

why: The letter names a material and a size and no town, and the town is the one thing the job already had. Asking for it again is asking a customer to repeat themselves, which is the whole complaint this rule answers.

name: a first letter with no job behind it is asked for everything

row.source_text: new floors how much for new floors in my house?

why: The thread that has said nothing yet is the case this rule must not change.

name: a staircase does not stop the floor being priced

row.source_text: hi, lvp in the living room and the stairs, 300 sq ft, kyle tx

why: The word stairs used to mark the scope unknown, which holds the whole email for a person -- so a customer who mentioned a staircase got no number for their floor either, and the floor was always perfectly priceable. The stairs are named in the quote at the firm's own rate per step and counted on site.

name: a quote that stops before the unit takes it from the letter

row.source_text: About 400 sq ft.

why: The model quotes the figure and sometimes stops before the words that give it meaning: a customer asked for the size answered "About 400 sq ft." and it came back quoted as "About 400". A number with no unit is refused, quite rightly, so the desk asked for the size, was given it, and asked again -- and the conversation could not end. The unit is in the letter whether or not the model quoted it, and the letter is what the gate already checks every quote against.

name: a unit from another sentence is not this number's unit

row.source_text: My neighbour did hers in square metres. Mine is about 400, whatever that is in your units.

why: Only what stands immediately after the quoted figure can be its unit. Reading the whole letter for any unit word would let a metre mentioned about somebody else's floor decide this one, and a wrong unit is worse than no unit: it prices confidently and wrongly.
